questions.question: A geologist breaks a small chip off a large quartz crystal. She measures the chip's mass and its volume to find its density, the amount of mass packed into each unit of its volume. How does the chip's density compare with the whole crystal's?
questions.answer: The same, since it is the same quartz
choices: The same, since it is the same quartz
Less, since it has far less mass
More, since it takes up far less space
Less, since a big crystal is packed tighter
questions.context: Density belongs to the material, not to the size of the piece. The chip has far less mass than the crystal, but it also takes up far less space, in just the same proportion, so every piece of quartz, big or small, has a density of about 2.65 grams per cubic centimetre.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade density lessons teach density as mass per volume, a property of the material that stays the same however small the piece, against the common belief that more material means a higher density.

questions.question: A student slowly pours three liquids that do not mix into a tall glass cylinder, one after another. After a few minutes they have settled into three separate layers. What decides which liquid ends up at the bottom?
choices: Which liquid is the densest
Which liquid is the thickest
Which liquid there is most of
Which liquid went in first
questions.context: Liquids that do not mix stack by density: the densest sinks to the bottom and the least dense rises to the top, whatever order they went in and however much there is of each. Thickness is a different property, for oil is far thicker than water yet floats on it, which is why spilled oil spreads over the sea as a slick.
questions.grade_note: G6.P4 names liquids of different densities stacking in layers (oil on water); the layered column is the standard 6th-grade lab, and taking a thick liquid for a dense one is the usual mix-up.

questions.question: Mercury is a metal, but it is liquid at room temperature. A chemist sets a solid iron bolt on a dish of mercury, and the bolt floats on it. Why does the iron float?
choices: Mercury is denser than iron
Iron is denser than mercury
Mercury's surface skin holds it up
Mercury pulls on it like a magnet
questions.context: Iron's density is about 7.9 grams per cubic centimetre and mercury's about 13.5, so the iron is less dense than the liquid and floats, held up by buoyancy just as a cork is held up by water. Gold, at about 19.3, is denser than mercury and sinks in it, and a magnet does not pull on mercury at all.
questions.grade_note: G6.P4 asks students to compare a substance's density with various fluids, not only water; a metal floating on a denser liquid metal is the floating rule applied to a fluid other than water.

questions.question: Ice is less dense than liquid water, so in winter a lake freezes over at the top while fish swim on in the water below. If ice were denser than liquid water instead, what could happen to a shallow lake in a long, hard winter?
questions.answer: Ice would sink, and the lake could freeze from the bottom up
choices: Ice would sink, and the lake could freeze from the bottom up
Ice would still float, and the lake would freeze over as now
Ice would melt at once, and the lake could never freeze
Ice would float lower, and the lake would freeze more slowly
questions.context: Most substances are denser as solids than as liquids. If water were too, ice forming at the cold surface would sink and pile up from the bottom until a shallow lake froze solid. Instead water expands by about 9 percent as it freezes, so its ice floats as a lid that slows the loss of heat, and the water beneath usually stays liquid all winter.
questions.grade_note: That ice floats because it is less dense than liquid water is in the unit's scope, and 6th-grade lessons draw its consequence: a lake freezes over at the top, with living water below.

questions.question: A girl lies back and floats, first in a freshwater lake and then, a week later, in the sea. In which does she float higher in the water, and why?
questions.answer: In the sea, as salt water is denser
choices: In the sea, as salt water is denser
In the lake, as fresh water is denser
In the sea, as its waves lift her up
In the lake, as its water is calmer
questions.context: Salt dissolved in seawater adds mass without adding as much volume, so seawater is denser than fresh water, about 1.025 grams per cubic centimetre against 1.000. The denser the water, the less of it a floating body must push aside to be held up, so she floats higher in the sea, and higher still in a lake about ten times saltier than the sea.
questions.grade_note: G6.P4 names a person floating more easily in salt water than in fresh water as a 6th-grade density case.

questions.question: A solid block of steel sinks in water at once. Yet a cargo ship built from thousands of tonnes of steel floats, even with a full load. What lets the ship float?
questions.answer: Its air-filled hull makes it less dense than water
choices: Its air-filled hull makes it less dense than water
Its steel is a special kind, less dense than water
Its engines push it upward as well as forward
Its flat bottom rests on the water's surface skin
questions.context: Steel is nearly eight times as dense as water, so a solid block of it sinks. A ship's steel is spread thin around a huge hollow hull full of air, so the ship as a whole, steel and air together, is less dense than water and floats. If the hull floods, water takes the place of the air, and the ship sinks.
questions.grade_note: The unit's scope names the steel ship: 6th-grade density lessons explain that its hull holds so much air that the ship as a whole is less dense than water.

questions.question: A girl lets go of a balloon filled with helium, and it rises into the sky until it is out of sight. Why does the balloon rise?
questions.answer: Helium is far less dense than air
choices: Helium is far less dense than air
Helium has no weight at all
Helium is warmer than the air around it
Every gas floats up through the air
questions.context: Air is a fluid too. Helium has weight, but it is only about a seventh as dense as air, so a balloon of it, rubber and all, floats up through the air as a cork floats up through water, with no need of heat as a hot-air balloon has. Not every gas rises: carbon dioxide is denser than air and flows along the ground.
questions.grade_note: G6.P4 is density across fluids, and air is one: 6th-grade density lessons explain the helium balloon by helium being less dense than air, against the belief that gases weigh nothing.

questions.question: After an undersea volcano erupts, a raft of grey, rough pumice stones floats on the ocean's surface. Most kinds of rock sink in water at once. What makes pumice float?
questions.answer: Its many gas bubbles make it less dense than water
choices: Its many gas bubbles make it less dense than water
Its glassy stone is itself less dense than water
Its heat from the volcano carries it to the top
Its rough surface catches the water and holds it up
questions.context: Pumice forms when frothy, gas-rich lava cools so fast that its bubbles are trapped, and the holes can make up most of the stone. The glass between them is denser than water, but with so much gas inside, the stone as a whole is less dense and floats. Rafts of it can drift for months or years, until water fills the holes and they sink.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade rock lessons name pumice as the rock that floats, and density lessons explain why: its gas bubbles make the whole stone less dense than water.
